name: Content creation & copywriting
blurb: Copy that converts, articles and newsletters that get read, brand voice, repurposing, and edits that strip AI tells.
searches: signs of AI writing new patterns humanizer skill update
landing page copywriting conversion test results headline
content strategy AI search citation LLM visibility technique
brand voice guide tone of voice AI content workflow
newsletter growth Substack Beehiiv strategy new feature

tests.prompt: Humanize this paragraph without changing its facts: "In today's fast-paced world, our platform isn't just a tool — it's a game-changer. It seamlessly empowers teams to unlock productivity, foster collaboration, and drive innovation. The result? Teams ship 2x faster. No setup, no training, no hassle."
tests.good: Removes the era opener, contrast reveal, em dash, triad, self-answered question and negation list; keeps the 2x claim without inventing new numbers or customers; no dashes added; says what the product actually does or flags [NEED: ...] where the source gives no specifics; short audit of what changed.

tests.prompt: Write the hero section for a landing page for an invoicing app for freelance designers. We have 3,200 users and invoices get paid 9 days faster on average. Give me headline options and a CTA.
tests.good: Asks for or states assumptions about the one action and differentiator; 5-10 headline variants across angles using only the given facts (3,200 users, 9 days faster); one stated pick with a reader-feeling reason; subhead of 1-2 sentences; CTA in verb + outcome form (not 'Sign up'); a risk reducer; no em dashes, contrast reveals or negation lists; no invented testimonials.

tests.prompt: Turn my 1,800-word blog post about switching our team to async standups into a LinkedIn post, an X thread and a newsletter section. Keep my voice.
tests.good: Extracts 3-7 standalone insights and assigns one idea per output; LinkedIn hook in the first two lines and 3-5 short paragraphs; X posts under 280 chars each advancing the argument; newsletter section opens on the point; no identical copy across platforms; no claims beyond the source; no engagement bait; notes that a voice sample or profile is used or requested.

tests.prompt: Write a 1,500-word blog post on how small accounting firms can shorten month-end close, in our voice (three past posts attached). It should rank for 'month-end close checklist', and I need a LinkedIn post to promote it.
tests.good: States a short plan first: voice and article here (brand-voice.md, long-form-articles.md, humanize-ai-writing.md), search intent, title and meta through seo (keywords-content.md: check the SERP for intent, one primary keyword, no stuffing), the promo post through linkedin-automation (post-writing.md: hook in the first lines, link in the first comment, run the pre-publish lint). Builds a voice profile from the three posts; leads with the point; invents no statistics or client stories and flags [NEED: ...]; runs the AI-tell audit; checks the Done means of all three crafts.

tests.prompt: I've finished a 1,800-word article in markdown with a title, an excerpt and a hero image file. Publish it to my self-hosted WordPress site as a draft, put it in the 'Guides' category with two tags, set the featured image, fill in the SEO title and meta description for Yoast, and schedule it for next Tuesday at 9am my time. Walk me through how you'll authenticate and what you'll send.
tests.good: Uses the WordPress REST API (POST /wp-json/wp/v2/posts and /media), authenticating with an Application Password over HTTPS and keeping it out of the chat and out of files; converts markdown to Gutenberg-safe HTML and uploads the hero image to /media first, then sets featured_media with alt text; resolves the 'Guides' category and tag ids (creating a tag only after confirming) rather than assuming them; Yoast's REST API is read-only (it adds yoast_head and yoast_head_json to responses; GET /wp-json/yoast/v1/get_head?url= returns the head), so those cannot be used to set the SEO title or description. Writing them needs the site's SEO meta keys registered with show_in_rest (register_meta/register_post_meta) and sent in the post's meta, or the user pastes the two strings into the Yoast box; never invent a field.; creates the post as status 'draft' first and uses status 'future' with a date_gmt converted from the user's timezone for scheduling; shows the user the exact payload and slug and asks for confirmation before anything is set to publish or schedule; returns the edit URL for review.

tools.name: WordPress
tools.why: W3Techs (Oct 2026) puts WordPress on 40.1% of all websites and 58.6% of the CMS market, nearly 7x the next CMS; HubSpot's 2026 content-tools round-up lists it as the default blog CMS.

tools.name: Google Docs
tools.why: The default drafting, review and comment surface for marketing teams; Google Workspace is the first suite named in the brief and has a first-party Workspace CLI (31k GitHub stars) with Docs write commands.

tools.name: Grammarly
tools.why: Described as the most widely adopted writing-polish tool in 2026 content-tool round-ups; its developer docs list Writing Score, AI Detection (beta) and Plagiarism Detection (beta) APIs.

tools.name: Notion
tools.why: Common editorial calendar, brief and drafting workspace for content teams; Notion is on the brief's big-suite list and hosts an official MCP server at mcp.notion.com (Notion docs, 2026 setup guides).

tools.name: HubSpot Content Hub
tools.why: A 2026 HubSpot round-up and a web search of the same topic both name HubSpot as the platform most used by growing businesses for content marketing; its blog posts API creates, schedules and publishes posts (needs the content scope).

tools.name: Semrush
tools.why: HubSpot's and other 2026 round-ups name Ahrefs and Semrush as the two leading SEO and content research suites; Semrush's API docs now include an official MCP section covering Claude.

tools.name: Ahrefs
tools.why: Named with Semrush as the market-leading SEO suite in 2026 content-tool round-ups; Ahrefs publishes an official MCP server for Claude (docs.ahrefs.com).

tools.name: Substack
tools.why: The leading newsletter publishing platform and already named in the craft's newsletter guide; it has no official public publishing API, so agents need a manual or unofficial workflow.

tools.name: beehiiv
tools.why: The main Substack alternative for newsletters and already named in the newsletter guide; has a public API and MCP reference at developers.beehiiv.com.

tools.name: Ghost
tools.why: Open-source publishing and newsletter platform with a stable Admin API (posts add/edit, JWT tokens); named by 2026 round-ups for newsletters and paid content, though only about 0.1% of sites (W3Techs).

tools.name: Webflow
tools.why: About 0.8% of sites (W3Techs) but common for marketing-team blogs; listed in the Claude connector directory and has an official MCP server and official skills.

tools.name: Surfer
tools.why: Surfer, Clearscope and MarketMuse are the standard SEO content-optimisation editors in 2026 stacks; Surfer shipped API v2 and an official MCP in 2026.

tools.name: Vale
tools.why: Open-source (MIT, 6.2k stars) markup-aware prose linter that teams use to enforce a style guide in CI; fits enforcing a TONE.md.

tools.name: Canva
tools.why: Content teams use it for carousels and social graphics that accompany repurposed copy; official Claude connector and official Apache-2.0 skills (graphics are mainly image-creation's job).

tools.name: Sanity
tools.why: One of the leading headless CMSs for structured content (Contentful the other); has an official MCP server and an MIT agent-toolkit with content-modeling and SEO skills.

tools.name: Wix
tools.why: Second-largest site builder after WordPress by site count (W3Techs about 4.2% of all sites, as the researcher noted); many small-business blogs live on it. The earlier 'no usable content API' reason is wrong: Wix's official hosted MCP (mcp.wix.com, remote MCP for Claude) calls site REST APIs including Blog draft posts, and Wix's official skills include a create-blog-posts recipe.

tools.name: Hemingway Editor
tools.why: 2026 writing-tool comparisons name Grammarly plus Hemingway as the standard free pairing for bloggers and content writers, with Hemingway the pick for readability (grade level, long sentences, passive voice, adverbs). Web and desktop app with a paid AI tier (Editor Plus); no public API, so agents reproduce its checks rather than call it. Left out earlier only because the bundled scorer covers readability.

tools.name: Clearscope
tools.why: Called 'the enterprise standard for SEO content optimization' in 2026 tool round-ups and named with Surfer and MarketMuse as the content-grading editors; customers on its site include Adobe, Shopify, Intuit, Conde Nast and IBM. No public API or MCP found, so it is a manual step (Google Docs and WordPress add-ons) that writers paste drafts into.

tools.name: Asana
tools.why: Editorial calendars and content production workflows run in work-management tools; 2026 content-calendar round-ups (Asana, Airtable, ClickUp, theCMO) list Asana, monday.com, Trello, Airtable and CoSchedule beside Notion. Asana has an official MCP (mcp.asana.com/v2/mcp) and a Claude app that creates tasks and projects, so an agent can turn a calendar into assigned briefs.

tools.name: Contentful
tools.why: With Sanity, the leading headless CMS for enterprise marketing content; previously folded under Sanity as a second skill, listed on its own here because teams on Contentful draft, localise and publish entries through its Management API. Official MIT MCP server for the Management API (contentful/contentful-mcp-server) and official MIT skills. Docs page returned HTTP 429 when fetched; MCP and skills confirmed via GitHub.

tools.name: Originality.ai
tools.why: The AI-detection and plagiarism checker that publishers and content agencies use to screen freelance and AI-assisted drafts (2026 reviews: fast.io, Cybernews); clients often judge 'sounds like AI' by its score, which ties to the humanize guide. Paid REST API (scan, batch scan, scan URL, results).
